processing: Pan-fixed at high heat, then rolled and shaped by hand-style pressing and rubbing until the strands are straight and needle-like; dried by air or sun and re-baked before leaving the factory to lift the aroma.
harvest_season: Picked young, about 70% one bud with one leaf and 30% one bud with a just-opening second leaf. The picking month is not well documented; spring is usual for Yunnan greens of this type.
appearance_dry: Tight, straight, glossy needles of a blackish green, with visible down.
taste_profile: Mellow and fresh with a rich clean aroma, heavier in body than the fine needle shape suggests.

brewing.notes: Ordinary starting points for a large-leaf needle green. Large-leaf material turns astringent sooner than eastern greens, so go cooler or shorter if it bites.

vintage_note: As is usual for Chinese green teas, buy it from the current year's picking and drink it within the year. Little is documented about how Mojiang Yunzhen is graded or priced today, so ask for the picking date.
description:
Mojiang Yunzhen is a needle-shaped green tea from Mojiang Hani Autonomous County in Pu'er. The name means roughly cloud needle: straight, tight strands, dark green and downy, made from Yunnan's large-leaf tea plant.

The shape is the work. After a high-heat pan fixing the leaf goes through several kinds of rolling and rubbing to pull it straight and thin, then dries by air or sun with a final re-bake for aroma. Its past as a steamed tea is long gone from the method.

In the cup it is yellow-green and clear, with a rich clean fragrance and a mellow, fresh taste. Treat it like a sturdy green: moderately hot water and fairly short steeps, because large-leaf tea can turn sharp if left too long.

This is a little-exported regional tea. Look for even, straight, unbroken needles with a dark sheen; broken pieces or dull colour suggest an old or low lot.
history:
An unusual origin for a Yunnan tea: the regional account says Japanese technique was brought to Mojiang in 1945 and the tea was first made in imitation of gyokuro, even called 玉露茶. In 1958 the process moved from steam fixing to pan fixing, changing its style.

It took the name Yunzhen in 1975, was rated a quality product in its prefecture for three years running, and in 1984 was listed among Yunnan's six famous teas. Little else is documented about who developed it.
